fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces the target WTaTiVZr-versus-commercial-tungsten comparison with a hypothetical fine-grained-versus-coarse-grained same-composition comparison.

It attributes plasticity and toughness to diffusion-assisted grain-boundary sliding, whereas the target interpretation centers on multicomponent solid-solution/lattice-distortion strengthening and Ti-V-Zr-assisted dislocation behavior, cohesion, localized plasticity, and crack impediment.
The predicted reduction in toughness is opposite to the target result, in which WTaTiVZr had substantially greater scratch-derived toughness and less cracking than tungsten.
The cited evidence does not establish that increasing high-energy boundary fraction lowers toughness in the proposed fusion-relevant materials.
explanation: The response addresses the broad fusion-materials question and supplies a clear, falsifiable experiment, but it does not reconstruct the target material, processing, test conditions, mechanism, or outcomes. Its controlled same-composition grain-size comparison is reasonably discriminating, although grain refinement changes boundary area, boundary character, and other microstructural variables simultaneously, and direct diffusivity measurements would be needed to establish the proposed causal chain. E1/E2 support high-temperature grain-boundary slip only in a different Ti-Nb-Ta-Zr-Mo alloy studied by molecular dynamics; they do not support the toughness claim or isolate boundary energy. E4 instead reports beneficial grain-boundary strengthening from TiC in tungsten, while E3 reports dislocation-controlled high-temperature deformation. Thus the proposal is a testable and potentially plausible alternative under restricted creep-like conditions, but it is weakly evidenced and has essentially no agreement with the hidden paper's specific reconstruction.
